title: The paradox of production: Surface water supply drives agricultural productivity but not prosperity in California’s San Joaquin Valley
c2_note: Under the plain/literal wording of Criterion 2, the paper examines legal and institutional water governance factors (California's pre-1914 vs. post-1914 appropriative surface water rights, Wright Act formation eras, 1909 irrigation district land-value taxation, and agricultural irrigation district boundaries). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is NOT met (c2 = no) because those water-rights and taxation rules govern agricultural irrigation supply rather than household or community water/sanitation service access, domestic and municipal water agencies are excluded, and a DAC's geographic location inside vs. outside an agricultural irrigation district boundary is not a rule-type mechanism governing domestic water service access (as the authors note, irrigation districts were established for agricultural water and not to govern community drinking water). Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study is still excluded (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because it fails Criteria 1 and 4.
rationale: Excluded as E07 (Wrong service). The study analyzes agricultural irrigation districts on California's San Joaquin Valley floor and explicitly excludes domestic, municipal, and water conservation water agencies (PDF Page 8). Its legal/institutional analysis of pre-1914 vs. post-1914 surface water rights and historical formation eras governs agricultural irrigation water supply and groundwater reliance rather than household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access (failing Criterion 1 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type scope of Criterion 2). Although a secondary analysis compares disadvantaged communities located inside vs. outside agricultural irrigation district boundaries (97 ID-DACs vs. 56 GDCs), irrigation districts do not govern domestic drinking-water service (PDF Page 14), and the only water-related metrics reported for DACs are CalEnviroScreen 4.0 environmental contamination/hazard percentiles (Poor Drinking Water Exposure (%) and Threats to Groundwater (%)) rather than household or community water service access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcomes (failing Criterion 4; statistical significance in Table 1 plays no role in this decision).

title: Divided infrastructure: legal exclusion and water inequality in an urban slum in Mumbai India
c2_note: Satisfies Criterion 2 under BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines a legal and administrative factor (legal recognition / slum notification status). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly analyses rule-type mechanisms governing municipal water service access: legal eligibility rules under the Maharashtra Slum Areas Act of 1971, pre-2000 residence cut-off documentation requirements (e.g. voter ID card), state vs. central government land-tenure rules, group application requirements for municipal community water taps, and municipal officials' discretion in operationalizing notification at neighbourhood vs. household levels.
rationale: This empirical quantitative study directly evaluates how legal exclusion (non-notified vs. notified legal status under the Maharashtra Slum Areas Act, pre-2000 documentation rules, and municipal application/discretion rules) shapes household water access, infrastructure availability, reliability, cost, and quantity (LPCD) across 593 randomly sampled slum households in Mumbai, India. All inclusion criteria (c1-c6) are clearly satisfied under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2, and quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals are reported.

title: Getting on the grid: A field experiment on bottom-up political pressure and access to essential public services
c2_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines bureaucratic, legal, policy, and political governance factors shaping municipal water access. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the study directly tests and analyzes multiple rule-type mechanisms governing service access: (1) administrative burden, application procedures, and documentation requirements via Treatment 1 (bureaucratic facilitation with group formation, proof-of-address certifications, evidence of slums' legal status, licensed plumbers' approvals, online portal submission, RTI requests, and negotiating eligibility and documentation rules); (2) formal legal and policy eligibility exclusions by land tenure/category under the 2014 Bombay High Court judgment, 2017 BMC water policy, and court orders barring connections on footpath, forest, and salt pan lands; and (3) bureaucratic and political discretion around multi-agency land-use No Objection Certificates (NOCs) and P-form approvals, interacted with Treatment 2 (bottom-up political coordination).
rationale: Full text matches record metadata (Gaikwad & Thomas, 'Getting on the Grid: A Field Experiment on Bottom-Up Political Pressure and Access to Essential Public Services'). The study satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1-c6) under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. It is a pre-registered factorial cluster-randomized field experiment in Mumbai's informal settlements examining how relieving household administrative and documentation burdens (proof-of-address, legal status documentation, licensed plumber sign-off, online portal filing, and negotiating eligibility rules), combined with bottom-up political pressure to overcome bureaucratic/political discretion in land-authority No Objection Certificate (NOC) clearances and bounded by formal legal/policy land-eligibility exclusions (2014 Bombay High Court ruling, 2017 BMC policy, and court orders on footpath, forest, and salt pan lands), affects verified household municipal piped water connections.

title: Household, neighbourhood and service provider risk factors for piped drinking-water intermittency in urban and peri-urban Zambia: A cross-sectional analysis
c2_note: Fails both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, no rule-type mechanism governing service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure) is examined: DHS home ownership (labelled tenure in S13 Table) is included solely as a household socio-economic/coping proxy (capacity to buy a storage tank) among households already using piped water; NWASCO regulator and IBNET utility datasets contribute only aggregate operational supply metrics (hours/day, LPCD, and non-revenue water percentage); and all 11 providers are commercial Water and Sewerage Companies entered only as unanalysed provider dummy variables alongside regional GDP per capita. Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2, the study also fails (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because regulator and utility data are used as monitoring data streams measuring water supply availability/loss rather than testing a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor, even though surface terminology mentions regulator reports, service providers, non-revenue water, and home ownership.
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although the study empirically examines piped drinking-water intermittency in urban and peri-urban Zambia using linked DHS household survey, IBNET utility, and NWASCO regulator datasets, it does not examine any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance mechanism governing water service access. Regulator and utility reports are used strictly as monitoring data sources supplying operational availability and water-loss metrics (service hours/day, LPCD, and non-revenue water percentage), provider variation across the 11 commercial utilities is modelled only via unanalysed dummy variables and regional GDP per capita, and household home ownership is included solely as a socio-economic proxy for household coping capacity among existing piped-water users rather than a tenure or documentation requirement.

title: Water and wastewater infrastructure inequity in unincorporated communities
c2_note: Satisfies both the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Plain wording: directly examines local legal jurisdiction and governance status (municipal incorporation vs. unincorporated county governance, annexation rules, and municipal extraterritorial planning jurisdiction). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: municipal incorporation status and legal municipal boundaries/extraterritorial jurisdiction (operationalized as Incorporated vs. Unincorporated Island, Fringe within the 1-mile municipal extraterritorial jurisdiction zone, and Outlying areas) constitute a legal-institutional and regulatory boundary structure directly governing utility service territories, annexation-linked service extensions, and community exclusion from municipal water and sewer systems rather than generic project delivery, behavioural promotion, or unanalysed macro-governance background. (While specific state/county annexation statutes are absorbed into random effects and discussed qualitatively, jurisdictional incorporation/boundary status itself is directly modeled as the primary exposure.)
rationale: This empirical quantitative study satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1-c6). It analyzes 31,383 U.S. Census block groups across nine states using multilevel negative binomial regression to test how legal-jurisdictional incorporation status and municipal boundary proximity/extraterritorial jurisdiction (Incorporated vs. Unincorporated Island, Fringe, and Outlying communities) govern exclusion from centralized drinking water and wastewater (sewer) service areas. It qualifies under both the plain wording and the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2 because municipal incorporation boundaries, underbounding, and extraterritorial jurisdiction are legal-institutional regulatory structures that directly govern utility service territories and community access to municipal water and sewer systems.

title: Institutional capacities for the universalization of access to basic sanitation; [Capacidades institucionais para a universalização do acesso ao saneamento básico]
c2_note: PASSES PLAIN WORDING / FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 READING. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 ('Examines a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), this study qualifies (plain=yes -> plain_criterion2_decision='include') because it examines municipal institutional capacity across financial, technical, operational, and political/planning dimensions, including binary indicators for whether a municipality has adopted a Municipal Basic Sanitation Plan (PMSB) and Municipal Basic Sanitation Policy (PPSB) pursuant to Law 11.445/2007. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, however, it fails (narrow=no -> decision='exclude', E03): the exposures are aggregate municipal state/resource and planning capacities (per capita operating revenues and expenditures, presence of municipal technical staff, waste workers and vehicles per 10,000 inhabitants, and general existence of a municipal sanitation plan/policy grouped via factor analysis into Capacidade Financeira, Técnica, Operacional, and Política). The paper does not examine a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access—such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership or regulatory structure directly governing service access.
rationale: Full-text Portuguese empirical article matching the record metadata. The study uses 2017 IBGE and 2018 SNIS municipal data for Minas Gerais to test how four dimensions of municipal institutional capacity (financial, technical, operational, and political/planning capacity) relate to municipal coverage rates of water supply, sanitary sewage, and solid waste collection. While it satisfies Criteria 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6—and would be included under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2—it is excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure) under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type scope of Criterion 2 because its exposures capture general municipal state, fiscal, staffing, operational, and high-level planning capacities (including binary existence of a municipal sanitation plan/policy) rather than a specific legal, regulatory, or administrative rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure directly governing access).

title: Effects of a community-driven water, sanitation and hygiene intervention on water and sanitation infrastructure, access, behaviour, and governance: A cluster-randomised controlled trial in rural Democratic Republic of Congo
c2_note: Passes the plain/literal wording of Criterion 2 (plain_criterion2_decision = include) because the bundled VEA intervention includes an institutional/governance component ('strengthening of village-level WASH institutions', electing a village WASH committee, signing an agreement with the Health Zone, and certifying 'Healthy Villages') and also measures a village-level water governance index as a secondary outcome. However, it FAILS the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (c2 = no): the exposure is a bundled WASH project-delivery, infrastructure-financing (US$2000 water + US$2000 sanitation grants per village), community-mobilisation, and behaviour-change intervention whose individual components cannot be disaggregated, rather than a legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure).
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). This cluster-RCT evaluates the Democratic Republic of Congo's national 'Healthy Villages and Schools' (VEA) WASH programme across 328 rural villages and clearly satisfies c1 (water and sanitation access), c3 (empirical RCT), c4 (improved water/sanitation access, collection time, quantity, and cost outcomes), c5, and c6. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 it would be included because the bundled intervention incorporates village WASH committee formation/strengthening and measures a village water governance index. Under the active 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope of Criterion 2, however, it is excluded because the exposure is a bundled donor/government project-delivery, infrastructure-grant, community-mobilisation, and behaviour-change package (whose mechanisms cannot be disaggregated) rather than a legal, administrative, tariff, tenure, eligibility, or regulatory rule-type mechanism governing service access.

title: Urban policy for poor areas and housing quality: An evaluation of the implementation of the Social Interest Special Zones (ZEIS) in Brazil; [Política urbana para áreas pobres e qualidade da moradia: uma avaliação da implementação das Zonas Especiais de Interesse Social (ZEIS) no Brasil]
c2_note: Plain reading: Yes — evaluates municipal urban land-use and regularization legislation establishing Social Interest Special Zones (ZEIS; Municipal Law 14,511/83, PREZEIS Law 14,947/87, Laws 16,113/1995 and 16,176/1996, and Federal Law 10,257/2001). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Yes — rather than generic physical project delivery or unanalysed macro-governance background, ZEIS operates through concrete legal and administrative rule-type mechanisms governing formalization and infrastructure access in informal settlements: (1) five statutory eligibility criteria for settlement designation (predominantly residential use, average household income <= 3 minimum salaries, lack/absence of basic infrastructure, density >= 30 residences/hectare, urbanizability); (2) requirement of a specific municipal law plus mapping and registration of households; (3) legal tenure regularization instruments (usucapiao on private land and Concessao de Direito Real de Uso on public land); and (4) regulatory accommodation via differentiated building/urbanistic parameters and lot-subdivision restrictions aimed at incorporating informal settlements under formal urban and infrastructure conditions. (Borderline nuance noted: ZEIS is a municipal zoning and land-tenure regularization regime rather than a utility-level tariff or connection-application rule, but tenure/formalization requirements, statutory eligibility rules, and regulatory accommodation directly governing formal network infrastructure incorporation fall within the protocol's rule-type scope.)
rationale: This full-text English empirical paper evaluates the causal effect of Recife's Social Interest Special Zones (ZEIS) legal zoning and tenure-regularization regime on household access to public network piped water and public network sewage services (plus bathrooms per household, garbage collection, and homeownership) across 1991-2010 census waves using PSM and Difference-in-Differences at the harmonized census-tract level. It satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1-c6), including Criterion 2 under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, as ZEIS operates through statutory settlement eligibility criteria, mandatory municipal law enactment with household mapping/registration, legal tenure regularization (usucapiao and Concessao de Direito Real de Uso), and regulatory accommodation of building/lot standards to incorporate informal settlements into formal urban water and sanitation infrastructure, rather than generic engineering project delivery or unanalysed macro-governance background.

title: The impacts of community-based water development projects on rural poverty among small-holder farmers: Evidence from the Ewaso Ng’iro North Catchment Area, Kenya
c2_note: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 but fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines an institutional/governance factor because Water Resource Users Associations (WRUAs) are localized collective-action water governance bodies institutionalized under Kenya's Water Act 2002 and Water Act 2016 (and land title is included as a covariate). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, however, the empirical exposure is simply binary household participation in community-based water development projects / collective action (WRUA membership vs. non-membership), with the Water Acts serving only as unanalysed macro-governance background. The study does not analyze any rule-type mechanism directly governing service access—such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements for service connection, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure. Land title is treated as a farm wealth/tenure-security incentive predicting voluntary group participation (and is embedded inside the Capacity sub-index of the composite Water Poverty Index), not as a tenure requirement governing water service access.
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 rule-type scope clarification for Criterion 2. Although the study examines rural household water security/poverty and water access indicators using 2019 survey data from 652 smallholder households in Kenya, its exposure is generic participation in community-based water development projects / collective action (WRUA membership vs. non-membership), with Kenya's Water Act 2002 and Water Act 2016 serving only as unanalysed macro-governance background. No rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure rules for water connection, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, discretion, or utility ownership/regulatory structure) is empirically examined. Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study would be included because WRUAs are institutionalized local water governance associations.

title: The effect of the regulation and regulatory enforcement on the implementation of the social tariff in the water sector: empirical evidence from Brazil
c2_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it examines sub-national water/sanitation tariff regulation, regulatory agency inspections, and municipal governance. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly analyzes rule-type legal and administrative mechanisms governing service affordability and subsidy access: (1) tariff and cost-recovery rules (social tariff category pricing and consumption caps under Regulation Arsae-MG No. 150/2021), (2) eligibility screening and documentation/administrative-burden rules (income thresholds, automatic enrollment without customer request under State Law No. 23,670/2020, and mandatory two-year CadUnico social registry updates), and (3) regulatory enforcement via periodic economic inspections of utility billing compliance.
rationale: Full text matches record metadata (Amorim et al., 2025, DOI 10.2166/wp.2025.193) and satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1-c6). It empirically evaluates rule-type legal, regulatory, and administrative mechanisms governing household WSS affordability access—specifically social tariff rules, CadUnico eligibility/documentation update requirements, automatic enrollment mandates, and regulatory enforcement inspections by Arsae-MG—on municipal-level social tariff enrollment among eligible low-income networked households across 572 Brazilian municipalities using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and GLS random-effects panel regressions. Both plain and narrow (2026-10-13) Criterion 2 readings clearly support inclusion.

title: Understanding the Cost of Basic Drinking Water Services in the United States: A National Assessment
c2_note: PASSES PLAIN WORDING / FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 READING. Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2 ('a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), this paper qualifies ('yes') because it tests municipal institutional, administrative, political, and regulatory variables as predictors of basic drinking water bills—specifically mayor vs. non-mayor municipal form of government, municipal government size (FTEs per capita), wholesale water purchasing, municipal fiscal conditions (revenue, debt ratio, utility spending), resident political ideology, and recent Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) health-based violations. Under the active 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope, however, it fails ('no'): utility ownership is held constant (all 2,119 systems are municipally owned and operated), state rate-setting and regulatory frameworks are unanalysed fixed effects rather than measured rules, tariff schedules are collapsed into the dependent price variable rather than tested as tariff or cost-recovery rules governing access, and the explanatory variables are general municipal political/organizational characteristics, financial balances, and water-quality/source conditions rather than rule-type mechanisms (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or ownership/regulatory structure directly governing household service access).
rationale: This empirical cross-sectional study analyses the drivers of monthly household bills for basic drinking water services (6,000 gallons/month) across 2,119 municipally owned US water systems using state fixed-effects OLS regressions. Under the literal/plain wording of Criterion 2, the study would be included because it tests municipal institutional, administrative, political, and regulatory variables (mayor vs. non-mayor form of city government, municipal FTE size, wholesale water purchasing, fiscal debt/spending ratios, voter political ideology, and past SDWA health-based violations). However, under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, it is excluded (E03, Wrong exposure): utility ownership does not vary (only municipally owned systems are included), state regulatory frameworks governing water rates are absorbed as unanalysed state fixed effects, tariff structures are collapsed into the outcome variable rather than tested as tariff or cost-recovery rules governing service access, and the explanatory variables represent general municipal political/organizational features, financial balances, and water-source/compliance conditions rather than rule-type legal or administrative mechanisms directly governing household service access.

title: Public enterprise pricing as redistributive policy
c2_note: Plain wording: Yes — alongside its primary socioeconomic predictor (local income inequality), the study explicitly examines an institutional/regulatory governance factor: utility ownership and rate-setting structure (local government-owned utilities whose rates are set legislatively by elected councils/boards versus private investor-owned utilities whose rates are set by state Public Utilities Commissions [PUCs] under quasi-judicial cost-of-service rules). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Utility ownership and PUC cost-of-service regulatory structure fall within the protocol's rule-type categories ('utility ownership or regulatory structure' and 'tariff or cost-recovery rules'), rather than generic project delivery, behavioural promotion, or unanalysed macro-governance background; however, in this paper they are modeled only as determinants/moderators of tariff structure progressivity (Unit Price Ratio) rather than directly governing a measured household service-access outcome, and the primary theoretical exposure is socioeconomic income inequality. Under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 reading of Criterion 2, the study is excluded because it fails Criteria 1 and 4 (wrong outcome).
rationale: Excluded under E04 (Wrong outcome). This political economy paper tests Cukierman and Meltzer's (1991) redistributive taxation model on 2019 single-family residential rate schedules across 1,183 large US community water utilities, examining whether local income inequality and public enterprise versus PUC-regulated investor-owned utility ownership predict tariff progressivity. Although utility ownership and PUC cost-of-service regulation are institutional/regulatory mechanisms, the sole modeled dependent variable is a policy/tariff-design metric — the Unit Price Ratio (UPR), dividing unit price at 30,000 gallons/month by unit price at 6,000 gallons/month. Because UPR cancels out overall price levels and omits household income, expenditure burden, basic bill affordability, consumption quantity, connection, continuity, and disconnection, the study examines determinants of tariff-structure progressivity rather than a water service access or affordability outcome (c1 = no, c4 = no). Statistical significance of individual coefficients played no role in this decision.

title: Water pricing and affordability in the US: public vs. private ownership
c2_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines institutional ownership (public vs. private utilities) and state regulatory governance. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, utility ownership (investor-owned vs. government/cooperative) and state regulatory/cost-recovery rules (PUC rate regulation of public utilities, and pro-private rate/cost-recovery rules in NJ and PA such as Distribution System Improvement Charges [DSIC] and fair market value legislation) are explicitly listed rule-type mechanisms ('tariff or cost-recovery rules' and 'utility ownership or regulatory structure directly governing service access') that directly govern household water tariffs and low-income service affordability.
rationale: This empirical cross-sectional study analyzes all 500 largest US community water systems using OLS regression to test how utility ownership (private investor-owned vs. public) and state regulatory structure (PUC regulation of public utilities and pro-private rate/cost-recovery rules such as DSIC surcharges and fair market value legislation in NJ and PA) affect annual household drinking water bills and water affordability for lowest-income-quintile households. It satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (utility ownership, regulatory structure, and tariff/cost-recovery rules directly governing household water affordability).

title: A study on the equity and influencing factors of local water supply services in Korea
c2_note: PASSES PLAIN WORDING / FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 RULE-TYPE READING. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), this paper would be included (plain_criterion2_decision = 'include') because it tests municipal political governance (mayor re-election), administrative-tier status (city si vs. county gun), and municipal fiscal capacity (degree of financial independence and per-capita local tax burden), and controls for operational consignment (민간 위탁) and local public enterprise status (지방공기업). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type clarification, however, it fails Criterion 2 (exclude, E03): the four focal independent variables (H1-H4) are macro electoral, urban-rural administrative-unit, and general municipal fiscal background characteristics rather than rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access. The two operational control variables—contracted O&M consignment (defined in Footnote 10 as K-water operational efficiency/modernization contracts targeting physical revenue-water/leakage ratios) and local public enterprise status (defined on p. 397 as operating an independent special enterprise accounting ledger vs. general municipal accounting)—are technical/accounting operational controls rather than utility ownership or regulatory rules directly governing household or community service access (noting that statistical non-significance plays zero role in this judgment). Likewise, average unit price and cost-recovery rate are modeled solely as dependent variables via Coulter inequity indices, not as tariff or cost-recovery rules governing access.
rationale: Full 15-page Korean article (with English abstract and tables) matches the record metadata (Ko 2024, DOI 10.3741/JKWRA.2024.57.6.393). The study empirically measures inter-municipal distributional inequity across 152 Korean local governments (2010, 2016, 2021) using Coulter's inequity index on six local water supply variables (including water supply coverage rate and average unit price) and runs Tobit and OLS regressions to identify influencing factors. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included because it examines political, administrative-tier, fiscal, and operational governance variables. Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, however, it is excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure): its focal exposures (mayor re-election, urban si vs. rural gun classification, municipal fiscal self-reliance, and per-capita local tax burden) are macro political, regional, and general fiscal background factors, and its operational controls (technical O&M consignment for leakage reduction and special enterprise fund accounting) do not analyze a rule-type legal, regulatory, administrative, tariff, or ownership mechanism directly governing service access.

title: Does local government proliferation improve public service delivery? Evidence from Indonesia
c2_note: PASSES PLAIN WORDING / FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 RULE-TYPE READING. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, local government proliferation (pemekaran, the administrative splitting of subnational districts into smaller local government jurisdictions under decentralization) along with exploratory indicators of local parliamentary political fragmentation and municipal financial audit opinions clearly constitutes an administrative, institutional, and governance factor (so plain_criterion2_decision is include). Under the active 2026-10-13 clarification, however, Criterion 2 requires a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership or regulatory structure directly governing service access) rather than macro-governance background or generic subnational administrative reorganization and public-works procurement corruption. Because district territorial splitting and general municipal political/audit governance do not examine a rule-type access mechanism or water/sanitation utility regulatory structure, c2 is no (exclude as E03, wrong exposure).
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope clarification. Although this empirical panel study measures household access to protected water and sanitation across Indonesian districts (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6) and would be included under the broad plain wording of Criterion 2 because subnational jurisdiction splitting (pemekaran) is an administrative/institutional governance factor, its exposure is macro-level territorial-administrative fragmentation and general municipal governance/public-works procurement corruption rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household water or sanitation service access.

title: Governance structures and their impact on tariff levels of Brazilian water and sanitation corporations
c2_note: Plain wording: Yes — examines institutional, regulatory, and governance factors including public versus private corporate management, state/micro-regional versus municipal regulatory agency oversight, rate-of-return versus price-cap/revenue-cap regulation, and increasing block versus uniform tariff structures. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Yes on mechanism type (utility ownership, regulatory oversight structure, cost-recovery regimes, and block tariff rules are formal rule-type mechanisms rather than generic project delivery or behavioural promotion), though in this paper they are analyzed only as determinants of corporate average revenue per m3 billed rather than rules directly governing household service access (social tariff reductions are explicitly outside the study's scope). Because the study fails Criteria 1 and 4 on outcome/access grounds, both the narrow and plain Criterion 2 decisions are exclude.
rationale: Exclude under E04 (Wrong outcome). Although Barbosa and Brusca (2015) empirically examine rule-type governance, regulatory, and tariff-setting structures across 51 Brazilian water and sanitation corporations (2005–2012), the study does not examine household or community service access (Criterion 1) and reports no outcome measuring access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, household affordability, or exclusion (Criterion 4). Its sole dependent variables (Lwt, Lst, Ljt) are corporate-level average billing yields (total annual bills divided by total billed m3 across all domestic, commercial, industrial, and public accounts), and the authors explicitly state in Section 4.1 that 'this paper uses not the concept of accessibility but the concept of tariff levels' (contrasting their metric with Oliveira 2008's affordability ratio) and note in Section 6 that social tariff reductions fall outside the scope of the study. Both the active narrow Criterion 2 reading and the plain Criterion 2 reading yield exclude due to failing Criteria 1 and 4.

title: Property Rights and Water Access: Evidence from Land Titling in Rural Peru
c2_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study evaluates a statutory property-rights and administrative reform (Legislative Decree 25902 establishing the Special Rural Cadastre and Land Titling Project, PETT). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, formal land tenure/property title and removal of registration/documentation barriers ('documentation or tenure requirements' and administrative hurdles) are directly analyzed as rule-type legal/institutional determinants governing household water and sanitation network connections by utilities/municipalities and households.
rationale: This English-language empirical paper meets all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Using data on 3,204 rural Peruvian households and a quasi-experimental modified difference-in-differences design, it tests whether formal land titling and removal of bureaucratic title-registration hurdles under Peru's PETT program (tenure/documentation status) affect household access to improved water sources, public water network connections, and public sanitation/septic connections, as well as utility versus household connection investment channels. Statistical effect sizes are also extractable for quantitative synthesis.

title: Ethnicity and government provision of drinking water infrastructure in rural China
c2_note: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain_criterion2_decision = include) but fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading (c2_legal_admin_factor = no -> exclude as E03). Under the plain broad wording, the paper examines institutional, administrative, and governance factors: the constitutional/administrative designation of minority autonomous counties and prefectures (Autonomous County, Autonomous Prefecture), co-ethnic county political leadership (Share Han Leaders), and decentralized local policy implementation under cadre performance evaluation timelines. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 scope clarification, however, the paper is a distributive-politics analysis of intergovernmental capital project delivery (where county ethnic demographics, general territorial autonomous status as a political/symbolic signal, and leader ethnicity predict MWR infrastructure project allocation across counties, explained via officials' preference for fast-to-complete, visible construction projects and lower informal transaction costs). It does not examine any rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community water service access—such as eligibility screening rules, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, frontline rule-application discretion or accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure.
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) applying the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification of Criterion 2. Although the paper empirically examines government provision of rural drinking water infrastructure in Guizhou Province (c1, c3, c4, c5, c6 satisfied) and passes the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2 (plain_criterion2_decision = include) because it analyzes regional ethnic autonomy institutions, co-ethnic county leadership, and decentralized cadre implementation incentives, its exposures are distributive-politics determinants of capital public-works project delivery (county ethnic composition, macro-territorial autonomous status as a general political signal, leader ethnicity, and career pressure to complete visible construction projects quickly) rather than a legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community water service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation/tenure rules, administrative burden, tariffs/cost-recovery rules, frontline rule-application discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure).

title: Financing Municipal Water and Sanitation Services in Nairobi’s Informal Settlements
c2_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it evaluates utility governance and enforcement interventions. Under the narrow rule-type reading, although the first experimental arm (tenant face-to-face engagement) is behavioural/outreach promotion, the second experimental arm directly tests systematic contract enforcement of utility service disconnection and cost-recovery rules for arrears—including stricter arrears eligibility screening, formal disconnection notices, financial hardship exemptions/flexible payment plan accommodations, physical service disconnection, and reconnection rules directly governing water and sanitation access.
rationale: This empirical study (cached as the July 2021 NBER Working Paper No. 27569 version of the same title and authors) meets all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Using a two-stage cluster-randomized field experiment in Nairobi's informal settlements, it evaluates systematic contract enforcement of utility disconnection rules for bill and connection-loan nonpayment—encompassing arrears eligibility rules, formal disconnection notices, indigency/hardship exemptions and payment-plan accommodations, and physical service disconnection and reconnection—and measures direct household and compound water and sanitation access outcomes (disconnections, reconnections, piped water and pour-flush sewer connections, working connections, main water source, metered consumption, water expenditure, and fetching time) alongside administrative payment outcomes. Null statistical effects on 9-month access outcomes do not affect eligibility.

title: What Determines Access to Piped Water in Rural Areas? Evidence from Small-Scale Supply Systems in Rural Brazil
c2_note: Satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study clearly examines institutional, governance, and administrative arrangements in rural water service provision (decentralized municipal provision vs. community water user associations, regional state-owned utilities, municipal user-participation mechanisms, and local political accountability). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, although parts of the paper frame the intervention around participatory vs. non-participatory project choice and political-economy accountability channels (media, elections, social pressure groups), the core exposure recorded in IBGE's National Basic Sanitation Survey (PNSB) and explored in the qualitative interviews is the legal/institutional service-provider and ownership structure governing ongoing rural piped water supply: water user associations (often operating under municipal concession contracts or formal co-investment conditions) implementing, operating, and maintaining systems versus local municipal governments/public firms (alongside models testing local municipal vs. regional state-owned CESB main utility ownership and switches). This falls directly within utility ownership or regulatory structure directly governing service access.
rationale: Barde (2017) is an empirical mixed-methods panel study in English evaluating how utility/provider ownership and management structure for small-scale rural water supply systems in Brazil (community water user associations operating systems—often via municipal concession contracts—versus local municipal government/public firm providers, alongside local vs. regional state-owned CESB main suppliers) affects rural household piped-water connection rates between 2000 and 2010. It satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1-c6) under both the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (utility ownership or regulatory structure directly governing service access).

title: Traditional Governance, Citizen Engagement, and Local Public Goods: Evidence from Mexico
c2_note: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 ('include') because it empirically evaluates a constitutionally recognized local governance/institutional regime (1995 Oaxaca reform recognizing traditional indigenous participatory governance, usos y costumbres, versus political-party electoral governance). However, it FAILS the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2 ('exclude', E03): formal municipal authority over water and sewerage and fiscal transfer formulas remain identical across all municipalities, and the exposure studied is general municipal political regime type (non-partisan community assembly leader selection and participatory public-works budget deliberation versus partisan elections), not a rule-type legal/administrative mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, service-level discretion/enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). A brief ethnographic background mention that historical community sanctions for refusing unpaid community service included water supply disruption is not empirically analyzed as an access mechanism.
rationale: Full-text empirical study matching the metadata. While it measures changes in municipal household water and sewerage coverage (c1, c3, c4, c5, c6 met) and passes the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 because it studies local institutional/governance regime type (usos y costumbres vs. partisan municipal elections), it fails the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Formal municipal service rules, powers, and federal infrastructure transfer formulas are held constant across municipalities, and the exposure is general municipal electoral/participatory political regime and public-works budget accountability rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household water or sanitation access. Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure).

title: Exploring the Influence of Participation on Programme Satisfaction: Lessons from the Ahmedabad Slum Networking Project
c2_note: Passes the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 because it examines participatory governance, CBO institutional activity, NGO-CBO partnership relations (d_ngo, active3, ngo_evl2), and CBO contact with municipal agencies (amc_com, amccntct) for post-project redress. Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading because its empirical exposures are post-upgrading community meeting attendance, NGO networking, and informal service-assistance contact in participatory project delivery rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (eligibility screening, documentation/tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, official discretion, enforcement, or regulatory/ownership structure). SNP's collective neighbourhood application and universal resident contribution requirements are mentioned only as invariant programme background on PDF Page 7 and are not empirically analysed. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, plain_criterion2_decision remains exclude because the paper fails Criteria 1 and 4.
rationale: Excluded (E04 Wrong outcome; also fails narrow Criterion 2 exposure scope). All 38 sampled slum communities had already received SNP physical upgrading as a sampling precondition, and the study measures post-delivery resident programme satisfaction and open-ended complaining behaviour ('social-psychological outcomes' that the authors explicitly distinguish from actual physical service provision and that conflate quality with quantity) rather than household or community water/sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion (failing Criteria 1 and 4). In addition, while the study passes the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 via participatory governance and CBO-NGO-municipal institutional contact, it fails the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type Criterion 2 reading because its empirical exposures are post-upgrading CBO meeting attendance, NGO partnership ties, and informal service-assistance requests rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (SNP's collective application and contribution rules are mentioned only as unanalysed background).

title: Monopoly Pricing as a Consumer Exaction in the Public Utility Sector: Monopoly Welfare Loss and Regulation in the Municipal Water Industry
c2_note: Plain wording: YES — examines a regulatory factor, comparing state public utility commission regulation versus local municipal regulation (by city councils or water commissions) of municipally owned water utility rate structures. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — regulatory jurisdiction over rate structures is analysed solely in relation to allocative deadweight loss (price-marginal cost markup) across aggregate utility residential revenues rather than as a rule-type mechanism directly governing household service access. Even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the study is excluded because Criteria 1 and 4 are not satisfied.
rationale: Excluded (E04: Wrong outcome; also fails c1 and narrow c2). Bruggink (1985) is an empirical public-utility economics study comparing state public utility commission regulation (n = 27) and local municipal regulation (n = 88) of U.S. municipal water utilities, but its sole outcome is the imputed Harberger deadweight allocative welfare loss triangle (divergence between price and long-run marginal cost combined with externally estimated regional price elasticities) expressed as a share of residential utility revenue. It does not examine water service access (c1 = no) and reports no outcome measuring access, connection, availability, reliability, observed consumption quantity differences, household affordability, or exclusion (c4 = no). Under the plain wording of Criterion 2 it examines regulatory structure, whereas under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading regulatory structure is not examined as a mechanism governing service access; under both readings the study is excluded because Criteria 1 and 4 fail.

title: Ensuring Sustainable Access to Drinking Water in Sub Saharan Africa: Conflict Between Financial and Social Objectives
c2_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines regulatory, financial-policy, and institutional governance factors in urban water supply (cost-recovery targets/benchmarks under corporatization and commercialization, public fiscal expenditure, and national/regional/municipal utility organization). Under the 2026-10-13 clarification, Criterion 2 explicitly encompasses 'tariff or cost-recovery rules' and 'utility ownership or regulatory structure directly governing service access': the paper specifically tests cost-recovery policy benchmarks and targets (operationalized via utilities' O&M cost-recovery ratio and its quadratic term to evaluate regulatory benchmark thresholds, alongside a robustness specification testing national, regional/state, and municipal utility governance structure in Model h4) and how cost-recovery rules create incentives or disincentives for extending formal water service access to unserved and low-income urban/peri-urban populations.
rationale: This empirical panel study of 75 urban/peri-urban water utilities across 25 Sub-Saharan African countries (1996–2012) satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1–c6). It examines drinking-water service coverage (c1, c4) as a nonlinear function of utility cost-recovery ratios and regulatory/policy cost-recovery benchmarks—as well as public water spending and national/regional/municipal utility institutional structure—directly testing tariff and cost-recovery rules governing service access under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (c2), using identifiable panel econometric methods and utility-level IBNET data (c3, c5) in English (c6).

title: Determinants and Benefits of Household Level Participation in Rural Drinking Water Projects in India
c2_note: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain_criterion2_decision = include) because it examines local participatory governance in community-driven rural water projects (household participation in village planning meetings/Gram Sabhas and household contributions toward project capital costs in villages with mandated Village Water and Sanitation Committees). Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading (c2_legal_admin_factor = no): the empirical exposure is self-selected household participation in generic community-based project delivery (voluntary attendance at planning meetings and donations of cash, labour, or materials, analysed through a social-movement/volunteerism lens), rather than a legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation/tenure requirements, administrative burden, connection tariffs or cost-recovery rules gating access, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). Project-wide rules (the 10% village capital cost-sharing mandate and VWSC structure) serve only as contextual background rather than a tested rule-level exposure, and non-contributing households were not barred by rule from accessing public water sources.
rationale: Prokopy (2009) empirically evaluates household participation in rural drinking water projects across 45 Indian villages, satisfying c1 (drinking water access), c3 (primary survey of 1,523 households using bivariate probit and propensity score matching), c4 (household water improvements index covering distance, collection time, reliability, adequacy, and perceived access), c5, and c6. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, it would be included as an examination of participatory community governance. Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type scope of Criterion 2, however, it is excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure): the evaluated exposure is voluntary/self-selected household participation in generic community-based project delivery (attending planning meetings and contributing cash, labour, or materials) rather than a legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism (such as eligibility rules, documentation/tenure requirements, administrative burden, or tariff/cost-recovery rules gating service access).

title: Is the Tap Locked? An Event History Analysis of Piped Water Access in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso
c2_note: Plain wording: Yes — examines housing/property tenure status (owner/co-owner, renting/co-renting, parents' or other's residence), formal urban land-zoning status (downtown, zoned periphery, non-zoned periphery), formal vs. informal sector employment, and policy periods across ONEA's institutional regimes (1985 'shared water management' prioritizing public standpipes; 1994 restructuring into a state-owned company governed by private law). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Yes (borderline) — although 75% of gains and 97% of losses occur via residential moves rather than in-situ connection changes, 25% of gains are in-dwelling new connections and 3% of losses are disconnections mostly for non-payment of water bills, and the Cox models directly estimate the effects and interaction of housing tenure status (Residence status) and formal land-zoning status (Zone of residence), where the authors explicitly note that connection to the ONEA piped network is not permitted/possible in non-zoned areas held via customary plot purchase from traditional chiefs prior to formal municipal zoning and plot allocation. Tenure status and formal land-zoning/tenure eligibility rules governing network connection fall within the rule-type mechanism scope.
rationale: This empirical event-history study analyzes gaining and losing on-plot/in-dwelling piped water access in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso using nationally representative retrospective life-history survey data (EMIUB 2000). It satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2: Cox proportional hazard models directly estimate the main and interactive effects of housing tenure status (owner/co-owner vs. tenant/co-renter vs. hosted) and formal urban land-zoning status (downtown, zoned periphery, and non-zoned periphery where plots are bought from customary chiefs prior to formal municipal zoning/allocation and where ONEA piped water connections are not permitted/possible), while also documenting in-dwelling new connections (25% of gains) and disconnections for bill non-payment (3% of losses). Confidence is medium rather than high because most observed transitions occur via residential mobility across housing/zoning strata rather than direct administrative screening of connection applications.

title: Money down the drain: Corruption and water service quality in Africa
c2_note: PASSES PLAIN WORDING / FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 RULE-TYPE READING. Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2 ('a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), utilities-sector corruption and bribery paid to government officials to obtain utility services clearly qualify as governance/administrative factors, so plain_criterion2_decision is 'include'. Under the active 2026-10-13 A16 scope clarification, however, Criterion 2 requires a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership or regulatory structure). Here, the exposures are self-reported illegal bribery to obtain water, sanitation, or electric services pooled together and the regional average of that utilities-corruption indicator, analysed as general/sectoral corruption degrading infrastructure and technical service quality rather than any formal legal or administrative rule, eligibility requirement, tariff rule, regulatory regime, or ownership structure.
rationale: This quantitative empirical study (Afrobarometer Round 7, N = 44,778 across 34 African countries) examines household water access outcomes (c1=yes, c3=yes, c4=yes, c5=yes, c6=yes), and would be included under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2 because utilities-sector corruption and bribery are governance factors. However, under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2, the study is excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure): its explanatory variables measure self-reported illegal bribery across pooled utility services (water, sanitation, or electricity) and regional utilities-corruption incidence as a governance/service-quality pathology, rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism (such as eligibility rules, documentation/tenure requirements, formal administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery rules, legal enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure) governing water access.

title: A small improvement: Small cities lag in expanding household water coverage across urban India
c2_note: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain=yes -> plain_criterion2_decision='include') because it empirically models administrative categories of urban local governments (municipal corporations, municipalities, town panchayats), per-capita intergovernmental infrastructure grant allocations (NURM/UIDSSMT), and a state-level fiscal decentralization index. Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (narrow=no -> decision='exclude', E03) because administrative categories and city size are used solely as proxies for general municipal resource/technical capacity, alongside macro fiscal decentralization and infrastructure grant funding, rather than any rule-type mechanism directly governing household service access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation rules, administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, discretion, or utility ownership/regulatory structure directly governing access; indeed the paper explicitly notes it lacks data on city-level institutional configurations for water service delivery).
rationale: This quantitative multilevel study examines 2001-2011 changes in household in-premise municipal tap-water coverage across 3,547 Indian cities and towns (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, c6). Under the broad/plain wording of Criterion 2 it would be included because it models local government administrative categories, intergovernmental grant transfers (NURM/UIDSSMT), and state fiscal decentralization. Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type clarification of Criterion 2, however, it is excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure): administrative categories and city size serve as macro proxies for municipal fiscal/technical capacity alongside intergovernmental infrastructure project funding and macro fiscal decentralization, without examining any rule-type mechanism directly governing household service access (and the author explicitly notes the absence of data on city-level institutional configurations for water service delivery).

title: Thirsty colonias: Rate regulation and the provision of water service
c2_note: Satisfies both the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines regulatory, institutional, and governance determinants of water service provision (rate regulation by municipalities and TCEQ, utility ownership/institutional form, and county subdivision regulation). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly tests rule-type mechanisms governing service access: tariff and cost-recovery rules (price regulation vs. pricing flexibility to charge cost-based capital recovery fees and rates in the absence of a statutory universal service mandate within Certificates of Convenience and Necessity), utility ownership and regulatory structure (municipalities, counties/general law water districts, non-profit water supply corporations, and for-profit private providers), and regulatory enforcement (county citations for lax enforcement of Model Subdivision Rules conditioning state infrastructure subsidy eligibility).
rationale: Full-text empirical econometric study examining how tariff/rate regulation, utility ownership and regulatory structure (under Texas CCN territorial rules without universal service mandates), subsidy eligibility rules, and county enforcement of Model Subdivision Rules affect central drinking water service coverage across 781 Texas border colonias. Satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2.
